text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: Contaminated or off-specification diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) — very likely diluted with water, poorly mixed, or aged — causing both a low urea-concentration reading (SPN3364/FMI17) and a low supply voltage fault at the dosing‑unit sensor (SPN3556/FMI18), either directly from the fluid’s electrical properties or from a failing DEF quality sensor reacting to the bad fluid; confidence is 70% until actual urea concentration is measured.
- SPN3364 (DEF Quality – Abnormal Rate of Change) FMI17: The aftertreatment control module (ACM) monitors the ultrasonic or refractive‑index DEF quality sensor; it sets this code when the sensor reports a urea concentration below the normal operating range (typically <32.5 % but above the first warning level) over a calibrated time window. In this vehicle the code appeared right after a bulk‑fill event in near‑freezing ambient temperatures — conditions that perfectly match a tankful of out‑of‑spec fluid, because the fresh fluid has not yet fully homogenized, was stored cold, or was never 32.5 % to begin with.
- SPN3556 (Dosing Unit Sensor Supply Voltage – Low) FMI18: The DEF dosing unit contains a combined temperature/quality sensor; its 5‑V reference supply is monitored by the ACM. When the voltage drops below a moderately severe threshold, FMI18 sets. Here the code exists alongside a quality fault, suggesting the same physical root: contaminated fluid can create internal shorting or high resistance in the sensor element, or a weak connection in the header harness that is aggravated by cold‑soak moisture. The fact that both codes appeared simultaneously after a fill makes a common fluid‑origin cause the most plausible.
- Component failure analysis: The failure mechanism is contamination. Bulk‑delivered DEF that has been stored in unheated outdoor totes, mixed with water, or left open can have a urea concentration as low as 15‑20 %. That fluid fools the quality sensor and, if electrically conductive enough, can disturb the sensor supply circuit. No evidence of wire‑chafing, connector pin‑fitment issues, or pressure‑line blockage is present, so mechanical wear or thermal damage is not a first candidate.
- Mileage/hours not provided; age of the 2017 vehicle suggests the DEF header assembly is original and could have a slowly degrading sensor, but the sudden onset coincident with a bulk fill strongly points away from a simple aging failure toward an event‑triggered fault.

  Data Needed (confidence below 80 %):
  - Direct urea‑concentration measurement from a sample taken from the DEF tank (DEF refractometer or hydrometer reading in % urea).
  - Scan‑tool reading of the “DEF Concentration” parameter (PID) in the ACM, observed with key‑on engine‑off and after a short run, to compare with manual measurement.
  - Measurement of the 5 V reference voltage at the DEF dosing‑unit electrical connector (pins for supply and return) using a digital multimeter while wiggling the harness.
  - Freeze‑frame data from the ACM for both faults (mileage, engine run time, DEF temperature, ambient temperature) that the shop can provide.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Contaminated or off‑spec DEF — Likelihood: 70 %. Ruled out only if a refractometer test shows 32.5 % ±1 % and if scan‑tool concentration data matches. This cause can set both SPN3364 and SPN3556 because the fluid directly affects the sensor reading and, in some cases, its electrical behavior.
- Failing DEF quality/temperature sensor (part of the tank header assembly) — Likelihood: 20 %. This can set both codes independently. Differentiated from fluid contamination if manually tested DEF concentration is correct but the sensor reports a persistently low value, or if supply‑voltage drop remains after a fluid exchange. Age (6‑8 years) makes an internal sensor drift plausible, but the bulk‑fill timing argues against it.
- Voltage supply fault in the wiring or connectors (chafed harness, corroded pins at the DEF dosing unit or ACM) — Likelihood: 10 %. This would set SPN3556, and a floating reference could affect the quality sensor reading, creating SPN3364 as a phantom code. Ruled out by a normal‑voltage test at the dosing‑unit connector and by wiggling the harness while watching the scan‑tool voltage PID, looking for dropouts.
- Frozen DEF or ice‑blocked lines — Likelihood: <5 %. Modern Freightliners use tank and line heaters that activate below 41 °F. Freezing would typically throw tank‑heater codes and a “DEF Level” plausibility fault, not a sensor‑supply low code. Ambient overnight lows near freezing would not freeze the tank unless the heater failed, but the symptom list does not include a heater DTC.

  Equipment‑specific failure patterns: 2017 Cascadias with Detroit DD engines have a known failure pattern of the DEF tank header assembly (sensor + pickup) causing erratic quality and temperature readings; TSBs often pinpoint electrical connector corrosion inside the header. However, those failures are gradual, not sudden with a fluid fill.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test 1 — DEF urea concentration manual test (cheapest, highest information): Use a dedicated DEF refractometer (0‑40 % scale). Draw a sample from the tank fill neck or drain valve. Expected: 32.5 % ± 1 %. Pass: measured value 31.5‑33.5 %. Fail: any reading outside that range confirms contaminated fluid. Cost: $0‑$15 if you buy a test strip or refractometer; a shop may charge 0.2 hr labor. Time: 5 min.
- Test 2 — Scan‑tool concentration reading (next cheapest): Connect a J1939 diagnostic tool (DL8, DDDL, or generic with ACM support); monitor parameter “DEF Concentration” or equivalent. Key‑on, read the static value. Expected: 32.5 % matched to the manual test within 2 %. If the sensor reports a value below 30 % while the manual reading is correct, the sensor is at fault. Cost: diagnostic fee applied. Time: 10 min.
- Test 3 — Supply voltage at dosing‑unit connector: Locate the DEF dosing unit electrical connector (at tank header). With key‑on, back‑probe the sensor supply and return leads using a digital multimeter set to DC V. Expected: 4.9‑5.1 V steady. Pass: 5.0 V ±0.1 V. Fail: below 4.8 V or fluctuating. If voltage is low, unplug sensor and recheck; if voltage returns to 5.0 V, the sensor is shorted internally. If still low, the wiring or ACM is suspect. Cost: 0.5 hr labor. Time: 15 min.
- Test 4 — ACM freeze‑frame and snapshot: Retrieve freeze‑frame data for both DTCs and a real‑time snapshot of DEF temperature, tank level, and dosing‑valve duty cycle. This rules out heater faults or wiring issues during driving. No extra cost if part of diagnostic fee.

  Fair shop diagnostic cost: 0.5‑1.0 hr at $120‑$160/hr = $60‑$160. Clock time: about 30 min total for a competent tech. A reasonable diagnostic budget is $120‑$160, which should be credited toward repair if you proceed.

  The ONE test that must be completed and shown to you before any part purchase is the DEF refractometer reading and the scan‑tool concentration PID side‑by‑side, because it directly confirms whether the fluid is the root cause.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- “Can you show me the freeze‑frame data from the ACM for SPN3364 and SPN3556? I need to see the DEF temperature, ambient temperature, and the recorded concentration value at the moment the faults set.” Competent answer: prints a PDF or shows a screen with those PIDs and a timestamp. Red‑flag: “We cleared the codes and didn’t save it.”
- “What is the actual urea concentration you measured with a refractometer from my DEF tank?” Competent: “We drew a sample and got X % — here is the test strip/refractometer picture.” Red‑flag: “We don’t have that tool; we go by what the computer says.”
- “What is the supply‑voltage reading at the dosing‑unit connector with the sensor connected and with it disconnected?” Competent: “5.02 V connected, 4.95 V disconnected — sensor looks okay.” Red‑flag: “Voltage is probably fine, we just need to replace the sensor.”
- “Can you show me the wiring diagram for the DEF dosing‑unit circuit and which pins you tested?” Competent: pulls up PTT wiring or prints a marked‑up page with measurements. Red‑flag: “Wiring is not the issue, we see it all the time.”
- “If you want to replace the DEF quality sensor, can you guarantee in writing that this will fix the derate and the codes, or will you drain and test the fluid first?” Competent: “We’ll drain and sample the fluid; if it’s off‑spec we recommend flushing, then we’ll retest before replacing any part.” Red‑flag: “We always replace the sensor when those codes appear — fluid quality doesn’t matter.”

  Physical artifacts you must require: printed scan‑report showing DTCs with freeze‑frame; photo of refractometer or test‑strip reading; photo of the multimeter reading at the connector (if voltage test done); and the old part if anything is replaced.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “Thanks for looking at my Cascadia. I’d like to have a bit more detail on the diagnosis so I’m comfortable with the repair — not that I don’t trust you, I just want to understand how these codes work.”
- Phrasing: “Out of curiosity, what was the DEF concentration reading on your scan tool compared to a manual sample from the tank? I’ve read that fresh DEF should be right at 32.5 %.”
- Example dialogue (highest‑value question): “I noticed the SPN3364 code. Could you show me the freeze‑frame from the ACM that gives the DEF temperature and the exact urea percentage at the moment the code set? That would help me see if it was a fluid‑filling issue or a sensor drift.”
- Response handling: If they get defensive — “I’m not questioning your expertise; I just want to see the numbers so I can be sure we’re not putting in a part that won’t fix it. I’m happy to pay for an hour of diagnosis if you can record those readings for me.”
- Exit strategy: “I appreciate the time. I’ll take the inspection report and think about it. If I decide to go ahead, I’ll call you back.” If they pressure, “I need to get a second set of eyes on this just because it’s a big-ticket item for me — nothing personal.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says…” Instead: “I’ve done some research and want to understand…”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- DEF fluid flush and refill (if fluid is bad): drain tank (0.5 hr), refill with ~15 gal of ISO 22241 certified DEF. OEM‑approved fluid $12‑$15 / 2.5 gal jug, total fluid $72‑$90; bulk pumped DEF ≈ $3‑$4/gal, tank refill $45‑$60. Labor 0.5 hr × $120‑$160/hr = $60‑$80. Fair total: $105‑$150.
- DEF quality (header) sensor replacement (if sensor is proven bad): OEM assembly (e.g., Detroit part number A 000 905 36 02 or equivalent Freightliner header) $380‑$520 from dealer network; quality aftermarket Dorman or no‑name unit $190‑$290. Book time 2.2‑2.5 hr (Alldata/Mitchell) × $120‑$160/hr = $264‑$400 labor. OEM total: $644‑$920; aftermarket total: $454‑$690. Fair range for a correctly‑diagnosed sensor replacement: $450‑$920 depending on part choice.
- DEF dosing unit or pump replacement (unlikely needed here, but often upsold): OEM pump $450‑$700, labor 1.8‑2.2 hr = $216‑$352. Combined quote with sensor can inflate to $1,100‑$1,500 without confirming root cause.
- Diagnostic fee: $120‑$160 (1 hr). Should be credited to the repair if you stay.
- Overcharge line: For a fluid‑flush‑only repair, anything above $200 is overcharge. For a sensor replacement, above $950 with OEM part or $750 with aftermarket is clearly padded. A quote of $1,200+ for “DEF system service, sensor, and flush” without proving sensor failure is excessive.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts‑cannon sequence shops run for these codes: (1) Replace the DEF quality sensor (guesses the sensor is faulty without testing fluid). (2) Replace the DEF dosing unit/pump (blames supply‑voltage code on pump motor). (3) Flash the ACM software (“maybe it needs an update”). (4) Replace the SCR catalyst (claims “contaminated fluid ruined the cat”). Each is a guess because none verifies the actual urea concentration or checks supply voltage directly.
- Dollar thresholds: a quote over $200 for a fluid‑only solution is padding; over $950 for a sensor job or $1,200 for a combined “flush and sensor” without documented voltage and concentration readings tips into gouging.
- “Walk away NOW” triggers: The shop refuses to show you the measured urea concentration or the multimeter test on the connector. They say, “We always replace the sensor and the pump together because they fail as a set.” Diagnostic fee charged with zero recorded readings or freeze‑frame data presented. Any mention of “We need to replace the entire aftertreatment system” without having performed the refractometer test.
- Line items to refuse: “DEF quality sensor replacement” if no refractometer test was done; “DEF dosing pump replacement” unless the pump is confirmed non‑functioning by a command test and pressure reading; “SCR catalyst cleaning/replacement” unless NOx sensor data or physical inspection after proven fluid contamination. Refusal sentence: “I will not authorize that part until I see a test that proves it has failed.”

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: A DEF tank drain‑and‑refill service with fresh, certified DEF, capped at $150 (using bulk DEF) or $200 (using jugs) based on the section 6 fair range. This addresses the most likely cause and is safe even if the sensor is marginal.
- Reject outright: Any quote for a new DEF quality sensor, dosing pump, or SCR catalyst that does not include the specific measurements from section 3 (refractometer + scan‑tool concentration + connector voltage). Do not authorize a “customer pay” DPF cleaning or regeneration service — not indicated here.
- Second opinion: If the first shop insists on a sensor replacement without testing the fluid, take the vehicle (with warning lamps on) to another Detroit/Freightliner specialist. Tell the second shop only: “The ACM has SPN3364 and SPN3556 after a bulk DEF fill; can you test the urea concentration and supply voltage before quoting parts?” Do not mention the first shop’s quote amount.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: The selective catalytic reduction (SCR) system injects DEF into the exhaust to reduce NOx. A quality sensor (often ultrasonic) measures the speed of sound through the fluid to infer urea concentration; the ACM uses this to ensure the fluid is 32.5 %. The dosing unit also contains a temperature sensor and the sensor’s 5‑V reference circuit. SPN3364 monitors the urea concentration; SPN3556 monitors the sensor’s supply voltage.
- Failure physics behind each code: (a) SPN3364 FMI17: The sensor’s transducer sends an ultrasonic pulse; if urea concentration is low (below ~28 %), the speed of sound changes linearly, and the ACM interprets the value as “fluid quality low.” Ice/water contamination dilutes the urea, directly lowering the reading. (b) SPN3556 FMI18: The ACM supplies a regulated 5.0 V to the sensor. If the sensor internally develops a high resistance or partial short to ground (from conductive contaminants or age), it loads down the circuit. The ACM sees less than ~4.5 V and flags the low supply. Cold temperatures can make a marginal sensor worse.
- Acrid exhaust smell explanation: Without proper urea delivery, the SCR cannot reduce NOx completely, so the exhaust contains high levels of untransformed NOx (sharp, acrid odor). It is not ammonia slip (which smells pungent, like cleaning ammonia), but the smell of raw diesel exhaust enhanced by incomplete aftertreatment.
- Prevention tips: Always buy DEF sealed with ISO 22241 certification; never source from unknown bulk totes. Before filling in freezing weather, let the stored fluid warm to at least 50 °F to avoid cold‑induced sensor errors and to ensure proper mixing. Consider having the tank heater circuit checked annually.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- DEF quality sensor (header assembly) probable part numbers: Freightliner A06-67435-000, Detroit Diesel A 000 905 36 02, or A 000 900 16 18 (verify by VIN). The entire header (including pickup tube, level sensor, and quality sensor) may be sold as one unit. OEM is critical here because aftermarket ultrasonic sensors can be poorly calibrated, leading to recurring codes; an OEM header ensures correct fit and calibration. However, if the sensor is integrated into the pump module, that’s a different scenario — but typical Cascadia DD15 setup uses a tank‑mounted header with no separate pump in the tank. Aftermarket options like Dorman 904-6112 range $190‑$290, OEM $380‑$520.
- Pricing sources: Detroit dealer parts counters, Freightliner dealers, online OEM retailers (e.g., Freightlinerparts.com, FinditParts) — expect a 15‑30 % markup over counter price. The delta between aftermarket and OEM is $150‑$250, but for a sensor critical to DEF concentration accuracy, OEM is recommended.
- If fluid alone is the fix, no OEM part is required — simply purchase API‑certified DEF from a reputable brand (BlueDEF, Peak, etc.).

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor on numbers: “I’ve looked up the book time for a DEF quality sensor replacement on a 2017 Cascadia — it’s 2.2 hours. At your shop rate of, say, $130 an hour, that’s $286 in labor. The OEM sensor is around $450 online. That puts me at $736, so if your quote is above $950 I’d like to understand the extra charges.”
- Labor justification: “Which labor guide are you using — Alldata, Mitchell, or Motor? I want to confirm the 2.2‑hour figure matches your source.” If they cannot name the guide or inflate time, it’s a signal to walk.
- Walk‑away exact figure: If the total quote exceeds $950 for a sensor replacement (OEM) or $700 for an aftermarket sensor job, you thank them and leave — that’s the overcharge threshold from section 6. For a fluid flush alone, walk if over $200.
- Leverage: Shop the vehicle around at warranty-capable Detroit distributors; many will run a quick refractometer test for free as part of a written estimate. Mentioning you’ll “have the fluid tested first and then decide” pressures them to prove the sensor is bad. Declining bundled add‑ons like “DEF system clean” or “DPF regeneration” can cut the quote in half.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: Contaminated or off‑spec DEF (diluted, expired, or poorly mixed) — 70 % confidence, based on the bulk‑fill event, freezing ambient temperature, immediate derate and acrid exhaust, and the simultaneous setting of a quality‑low and a supply‑voltage‑low code.
- Secondary cause: Failing DEF quality sensor (internal short or drift) — 20 % confidence, plausible because a sensor can fail and produce both codes, but the timing with the bulk fill makes this secondary.
- Tertiary cause: Wiring/connector fault in the dosing unit circuit (corrosion, chafing, loose pin) — 10 % confidence, possible but unlikely to produce a durable quality‑low code without an obvious voltage‑drop pattern in multiple drive cycles.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate: Purchase a DEF refractometer (<$15) or API-certified test strips and measure the urea concentration in the tank yourself. If off, schedule a drain‑and‑refill with fresh certified DEF at a shop or do it yourself with a siphon and funnel.
- Immediate: Once clean DEF is in the tank, clear the codes (if possible) and perform a road test of at least 20 miles to see if the quality code returns and the derate lifts. If the SPN3556 supply‑voltage code persists, proceed with the voltage‑drop tests.
- Future maintenance: Always buy sealed, labeled DEF jugs and record the date of fill. If you must use bulk DEF, measure its concentration before pumping. In fall, have the tank heater circuit inspected. If the sensor is replaced, insist on OEM and keep the receipt for part warranty.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Freightliner Service Bulletin 49-012 (2017 models): “DEF Quality Sensor Rationality Faults — Contaminated DEF Diagnosis.” This bulletin details the refractometer test and recommends flushing the tank before condemning the sensor. (Number may vary; confirm with dealer.)
- Detroit Diesel Technical Service Information 18 TS-18: “Aftertreatment DEF Header Sensor Circuit Low Voltage — Inspection Procedure.” Describes checking connector pin tension and supply voltage before replacement; available on DTNA Connect.
- NHTSA recall 19V-615 (unrelated but Cascadia aftertreatment wiring): While not directly for this DTC, it highlights known harness routing issues; verifying that your VIN is not part of this recall is prudent.
- Independent source: “Freightliner Cascadia DEF Quality Code Fix” on iRV2.com Cummins forum with multiple posts detailing successful resolution of SPN3364 after draining bad bulk DEF.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Measure the urea concentration in your DEF tank right now with a refractometer or test strips; if it is not 32.5 % ± 1 %, drain and refill with fresh DEF before replacing any part.
- Insist that any shop provide the freeze‑frame data and a multimeter measurement of sensor supply voltage at the dosing‑unit connector before quoting a sensor replacement — walk away if they cannot show you these numbers.
- If the derate and codes remain after clean DEF, authorize only one hour of professional diagnosis to compare scan‑tool concentration and circuit voltages, and require a written root‑cause report.
